entries.f50d92103243e547572b72a27261437d4eedc20e: <div sID="gen10061" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="33" osisID="Job.33" sID="Job.33"/> <div eID="gen10061" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10062" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen10063" type="x-p"/> Pompous prefaces, like the teeming mountain, often introduce poor performances; but Elihu's discourse here does not disappoint the expectations which his preface had raised. It is substantial, and lively, and very much to the purpose. He had, in the foregoing chapter, said what he had to say to Job's three friends; and now he comes up close to Job himself and directs his speech to him. I. He bespeaks Job's favourable acceptance of what he should say, and desires he would take him for that person whom he had so often wished for, that would plead with him, and receive his plea on God's behalf, <reference osisRef="Job.33.1-Job.33.7">ver. 1-7</reference>. II. He does, in God's name, bring an action against him, for words which he had spoken, in the heat of disputation, reflecting upon God as dealing hardly with him, <reference osisRef="Job.33.8-Job.33.11">ver. 8-11</reference>. III. He endeavours to convince him of his fault and folly herein, by showing him, 1. God's sovereign dominion over man, <reference osisRef="Job.33.12-Job.33.13">ver. 12, 13</reference>. 2. The care God takes of man, and the various ways and means he uses to do his soul good, which we have reason to think he designs when he lays bodily afflictions upon him, <reference osisRef="Job.33.14">ver. 14</reference>. (1.) Job had sometimes complained of unquiet dreams, <reference osisRef="Job.7.14">ch. vii. 14</reference>. "Why," says Elihu, "God sometimes speaks conviction and instruction to men by such dreams," <reference osisRef="Job.33.15-Job.33.18">ver. 15-18</reference>. (2.) Job had especially complained of his sicknesses and pains; and, as to these, he shows largely that they were so far from being tokens of God's wrath, as Job took them, or evidences of Job's hypocrisy, as his friends took them, that they were really wise and gracious methods, which divine grace took for the increase of his acquaintance with God, to work patience, experience, and hope, <reference osisRef="Job.33.19-Job.33.30">ver. 19-30</reference>. And, lastly, he concludes with a request to Job, either to answer him or give him leave to go on, <reference osisRef="Job.33.31-Job.33.33">ver. 31-33</reference>.
entries.d91dfb73d49b6bca1b5708a2f848ef9e075a1c7b: <div eID="gen10063" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen10062" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Address of Elihu. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1520.)</title> <div sID="gen10064" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Wherefore, Job, I pray thee, hear my speeches, and hearken to all my words. <hi type="super">2</hi> Behold, now I have opened my mouth, my tongue hath spoken in my mouth. <hi type="super">3</hi> My words <hi type="italic">shall be of</hi> the uprightness of my heart: and my lips shall utter knowledge clearly. <hi type="super">4</hi> The Spirit of God hath made me, and the breath of the Almighty hath given me life. <hi type="super">5</hi> If thou canst answer me, set <hi type="italic">thy words</hi> in order before me, stand up. 6 Behold, I <hi type="italic">am</hi> according to thy wish in God's stead: I also am formed out of the clay. <hi type="super">7</hi> Behold, my terror shall not make thee afraid, neither shall my hand be heavy upon thee. <div eID="gen10064" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10065" type="x-p"/> Several arguments Elihu here uses to persuade Job not only to give him a patient hearing, but to believe that he designed him a good office, and to take it kindly, and be willing to receive the instructions he was now about to give him. Let Job consider, 1. That Elihu does not join with his three friends against him. He has, in the foregoing chapter, declared his dislike of their proceedings, disclaimed their hypothesis, and quite set aside the method they took of healing Job. "<hi type="italic">Wherefore, Job, I pray thee, hear my speech,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.33.1">v. 1</reference>. They were all in the same song, all spoke in the same strain; but I am trying a new say, <hi type="italic">therefore hearken to all my words,</hi> and not to some of them only;" for we cannot judge of a discourse unless we take it entire and hearken to it all. 2. That he intended to make a solemn business of it, not to put in a word by the by, or give a short repartee, to show his wit: after long silence he <hi type="italic">opened his mouth</hi> (<reference osisRef="Job.33.2">v. 2</reference>), with deliberation and design. Upon mature consideration he had already begun to speak, and was prepared to go on if Job would encourage him by his attention. 3. That he was resolved to speak as he thought and not otherwise (<reference osisRef="Job.33.3">v. 3</reference>): "<hi type="italic">My words shall be of the uprightness of my heart,</hi> the genuine product of my convictions and sentiments." There was reason to suspect that Job's three friends did not think, in their consciences, that Job was so bad a man as they had in their discourses, merely for the support of their hypothesis, represented him to be; and that was not fair. It is a base thing to condemn those with our tongues, to serve a turn, whom at the same time we cannot but in our consciences think well of. Elihu is an honest man, and scorns to do so. 4. That what he said should be easy, and not dark and hard to be understood: <hi type="italic">My lips shall utterly knowledge clearly.</hi> Job shall readily comprehend his meaning, and perceive what he aims at. Those that speak of the things of God should carefully avoid all obscurity and perplexedness both of notion and expression, and speak as plainly and clearly as they can; for by that it will appear that they do themselves understand what they speak of, that they mean honestly, and design the edification of those they speak to. 5. That he would, in his discourse, make the best use he could of the reason and understanding God had given him, that life, that rational soul which he received from <hi type="italic">the Spirit of God</hi> and <hi type="italic">the breath of the Almighty,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.33.4">v. 4</reference>. He owns himself unfit to enter into the lists with his seniors, yet he desires they will not despise his youth, for that he is God's workmanship as well as they, made by the same hand, endued with the same noble powers and faculties, and designed for the same great end; and therefore why may not the God that made him make use of his as an instrument of good to Job? With this consideration also we should quicken ourselves (and perhaps Elihu made that use of it) to do good in our places according to our capacity. God has made us, and given us life, and therefore we should study to use our life to some good purpose, to spend it in glorifying God and serving our generation according to his will, that we may answer the end of our creation and it may not be said that we were made in vain. 6. That he would be very willing to hear what Job could object against what he had to say (<reference osisRef="Job.33.5">v. 5</reference>): "<hi type="italic">If thou canst, answer me.</hi> If thou hast so much strength and spirit left thee, and art not quite spent with the distemper and the dispute, <hi type="italic">set thy words in order,</hi> and they shall have their due consideration." Those that can speak reason will hear reason. 7. That he had often wished for one that would appear for God, with whom he might freely expostulate, and to whom, as arbitrator, he might refer the matter, and such a one Elihu would be (<reference osisRef="Job.33.6">v. 6</reference>): <hi type="italic">I am, according to thy wish, in God's stead.</hi> How pathetically had Job wished (<reference osisRef="Job.16.21">ch. xvi. 21</reference>), <hi type="italic">O that one might plead for a man with God!</hi> and (<reference osisRef="Job.22.3">ch. xxii. 3</reference>), <hi type="italic">O that I knew where I might find him!</hi> Only he would make it his bargain that <hi type="italic">his dread should not make him afraid,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.13.21">ch. xiii. 21</reference>. "Now," says Elihu, "look upon me, for this once, as in God's stead. I will undertake to plead his cause with thee and to show thee wherein thou hast affronted him and what he has against thee; and what appeals or complaints thou hast to make to God make them to me." 8. That he was not an unequal match for him: "<hi type="italic">I also am formed out of the clay.</hi> I also, as well as the first man (<reference osisRef="Gen.2.7">Gen. ii. 7</reference>), I also as well as thou." Job had urged this with God as a reason why he should not bear hard upon him (<reference osisRef="Job.10.9">ch. x. 9</reference>), <hi type="italic">Remember that thou hast made me as the clay.</hi> "I," says Elihu, "am <hi type="italic">formed out of the clay</hi> as well as thou," <hi type="italic">formed of the same clay,</hi> so some read it. It is good for us all to consider that we are formed out of the clay; and well for us it is that those who are to us in God's stead are so, that he speaks to us by men like ourselves, according to Israel's wish upon a full trial, <reference osisRef="Deut.5.24">Deut. v. 24</reference>. God has wisely deposited the treasure in earthen vessels like ourselves, <reference osisRef="2Cor.4.7">2 Cor. iv. 7</reference>. 9. That he would have no reason to be frightened at the assault he made upon him (<reference osisRef="Job.33.7">v. 7</reference>): "<hi type="italic">My terror shall not make thee afraid,</hi>" (1.) "As thy friends have done with their arguings. I will not reproach thee as they have done, nor draw up such a heavy charge against thee, Nor," (2.) "As God would do if he should appear to reason with thee. I stand upon the same level with thee, and am made of the same mould, and therefore cannot impose that terror upon thee which thou mayest justly dread from the appearance of the divine Majesty." If we would rightly convince men, it must be by reason, not by terror, by fair arguing, not by a heavy hand.
entries.df8f215a55ac2d4bd85f0c149f4be859ee60a1dd: <div eID="gen10065" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10066" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">8</hi> Surely thou hast spoken in mine hearing, and I have heard the voice of <hi type="italic">thy</hi> words, <hi type="italic">saying,</hi> <hi type="super">9</hi> I am clean without transgression, I <hi type="italic">am</hi> innocent; neither <hi type="italic">is there</hi> iniquity in me. <hi type="super">10</hi> Behold, he findeth occasions against me, he counteth me for his enemy, <hi type="super">11</hi> He putteth my feet in the stocks, he marketh all my paths. <hi type="super">12</hi> Behold, <hi type="italic">in</hi> this thou art not just: I will answer thee, that God is greater than man. <hi type="super">13</hi> Why dost thou strive against him? for he giveth not account of any of his matters. <div eID="gen10066" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10067" type="x-p"/> In these verses, <div eID="gen10067" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10068" type="x-p"/> I. Elihu particularly charges Job with some indecent expressions that had dropped from him, reflecting upon the justice and goodness of God in his dealings with him. He does not ground the charge upon report, but was himself an ear-witness of what he here reproves him for (<reference osisRef="Job.33.8">v. 8</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Thou hast spoken it in my hearing,</hi> and in the hearing of all this company." He had it not at second hand; if so, he would have hoped it was not so bad as it was represented. He did not hear it from Job in private conversation, for then he would not have been so ill-bred as to repeat it thus publicly; but Job had said it openly, and therefore it was fit he should be openly reproved for it. <hi type="italic">Those that sin before all rebuke before all.</hi> When we hear any thing said that tends to God's dishonour we ought publicly to bear our testimony against it. What is said amiss in our hearing we are concerned to reprove; for <hi type="italic">you are my witnesses, saith the Lord,</hi> to confront the accuser. 1. Job had represented himself as innocent (<reference osisRef="Job.33.9">v. 9</reference>): Thou hast said, <hi type="italic">I am clean without transgression.</hi> Job had not said this <hi type="italic">totidem verbis—in so many words;</hi> nay, he had owned himself to have sinned and to be impure before God; but he had indeed said, <hi type="italic">Thou knowest that I am not wicked, my righteousness I hold fast,</hi> and the like, on which Elihu might ground this charge. It was true that Job was a perfect and an upright man and not such a one as his friends had represented him; but he ought not to have insisted so much upon it, as if God had therefore done him wrong in afflicting him. Yet, it should seem, Elihu did not deal fairly in charging Job with saying that he was clean and innocent from all transgression, when he only pleaded that he was upright and innocent from the great transgression. But those that speak passionately and unwarily must thank themselves if they be misunderstood; they should have taken more care. 2. He had represented God as severe in marking what he did amiss and taking all advantages against him (<reference osisRef="Job.33.10-Job.33.11">v. 10, 11</reference>), as if he sought opportunity to pick quarrels with him. <hi type="italic">He findeth occasions against me,</hi> which supposes seeking them. To this purport Job had spoken, <reference osisRef="Job.14.16-Job.14.17">ch. xiv. 16, 17</reference>, <hi type="italic">Dost thou not watch over my sin? He counteth me for his enemy;</hi> so he had expressly said, <reference osisRef="Job.13.24">ch. xiii. 24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.19.11">xix. 11</reference>. "<hi type="italic">He putteth my feet in the stocks,</hi> that, as I cannot contend with him, so I may not be able to flee from him;" this he had said, <reference osisRef="Job.13.27">ch. xiii. 27</reference>. <hi type="italic">He marketh all my paths;</hi> so he had said, <reference osisRef="Job.13.27">ch. xiii. 27</reference>. <div eID="gen10068" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10069" type="x-p"/> II. He endeavours to convince him that he had spoken amiss in speaking thus, and that he ought to humble himself before God for it, and by repentance to unsay it (<reference osisRef="Job.33.12">v. 12</reference>): <hi type="italic">Behold, in this thou art not just. Here thou art not in the right,</hi> so some read it. See; the difference between the charge which Elihu exhibited against Job and that which was preferred against him by his other friends; they would not own that he was just at all, but Elihu only says, "In this, in saying this, thou art not just." 1. "Thou dost not deal justly with God." To be just is to render to all their due; now we do not render to God his due, nor are we just to him, if we do not acknowledge his equity and kindness in all his dispensations of his providence towards us, that he is righteous in all his ways, and that, however it be, yet he is good. 2. "Thou dost not speak the language of a righteous man. I do not deny but thou art such a one, but in this thou dost not make it to appear." Many that are just yet, in some particular instances, do not speak and act like themselves; and as, on the one hand, we must not fail to tell even a good man wherein he mistakes and does amiss, nor flatter him in his errors and passions, for in that we are not kind, so on the other hand we must not draw men's characters, nor pass a judgment on them, from one instance, or some few misplaced words, for in that we are not just. <hi type="italic">In many things we all offend,</hi> and therefore must be candid in our censures. Two things Elihu proposes to Job's consideration, to convince him that he had said amiss:—(1.) That God is infinitely above us, and therefore it is madness to contend with him; for if he plead against us with his great power we cannot stand before him. <hi type="italic">I will answer thee,</hi> says Elihu, in one word, which carries its own evidence along with it, <hi type="italic">That God is greater than man;</hi> no doubt he is, infinitely greater. Between God and man there is no proportion. Job had himself said a great deal, and admirably well, concerning the greatness of God, his irresistible power and incontestable sovereignty, his terrible majesty and unsearchable immensity. "Now," said Elihu, "do but consider what thou thyself hast said concerning the greatness of God, and apply it to thyself; if he is greater than man, he is greater than thou, and thou wilt see reason enough to repent of these ill-natures, ill-favoured, reflections upon him, and to blush at thy folly, and tremble to think of thy own presumption." Note, There is enough in this one plain unquestionable truth, <hi type="italic">That God is greater than man,</hi> if duly improved, for ever to put to silence and to shame all our complaints of his providence and our exceptions against his dealings with us. He is not only more wise and powerful than we are, and therefore it is to no purpose to contend with him who will be too hard for us, but more holy, just, and good, for these are the transcendent glories and excellencies of the divine nature; in these God is greater than man, and therefore it is absurd and unreasonable to find fault with him, for he is certainly in the right. (2.) That God is not accountable to us (<reference osisRef="Job.33.13">v. 13</reference>): <hi type="italic">Why dost thou strive against him?</hi> Those that complain of God strive against him, implead him, impeach him, bring an action against him. And why do they do so? For what cause? To what purpose? Note, It is an unreasonable thing for us, weak, foolish, sinful, creatures, to strive with a God of infinite wisdom, power, and goodness. Woe to the clay that strives with the potter; <hi type="italic">for he gives no account of any of his matters.</hi> He is under no obligation to show us a reason for what he does, neither to tell us what he designs to do (in what method, at what time, by what instruments) nor to tell us why he deals thus with us. He is not bound either to justify his own proceedings or to satisfy our demands and enquiries; his judgments will certainly justify themselves. If we do not satisfy ourselves in them, it is our own fault. It is therefore daring impiety for us to arraign God at our bar, or challenge him to show cause for what he doeth, to say unto him, <hi type="italic">What doest thou?</hi> or, <hi type="italic">Why doest thou so? He gives not account of all his matters</hi> (so some read it); he reveals as much as it is fit for us to know, as follows here (<reference osisRef="Job.33.14">v. 14</reference>), but still there are secret things, which belong not to us, which it is not for us to pry into.
entries.31e9d7ad8d7da85339af024aaa11888cd5d88229: <div eID="gen10069" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10070" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">14</hi> For God speaketh once, yea twice, <hi type="italic">yet man</hi> perceiveth it not. <hi type="super">15</hi> In a dream, in a vision of the night, when deep sleep falleth upon men, in slumberings upon the bed; <hi type="super">16</hi> Then he openeth the ears of men, and sealeth their instruction, <hi type="super">17</hi> That he may withdraw man <hi type="italic">from his</hi> purpose, and hide pride from man. <hi type="super">18</hi> He keepeth back his soul from the pit, and his life from perishing by the sword. <div eID="gen10070" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10071" type="x-p"/> Job had complained that God kept him wholly in the dark concerning the meaning of his dealings with him, and therefore concluded he dealt with him as his enemy. "No," says Elihu, "he speaks to you, but you do not perceive him; so that the fault is yours, not his; and he is designing your real good even in those dispensations which you put this harsh construction upon." Observe in general, 1. What a friend God is to our welfare: <hi type="italic">He speaketh to us once, yea, twice,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.33.14">v. 14</reference>. It is a token of his favour that, notwithstanding the distance and quarrel between us and him, yet he is pleased to speak to us. It is an evidence of his gracious design that he is pleased to speak to us of our own concerns, to show us what is our duty and what our interest, what he requires of us and what we may expect from him, to tell us of our faults and warn us of our danger, to show us the way and to lead us in it. This he does once, yea, twice, that is, again and again; when one warning is neglected he gives another, not willing that any should perish. <hi type="italic">Precept must be upon precept, and line upon line;</hi> it is so, that sinners may be left inexcusable. 2. What enemies we are to our own welfare: <hi type="italic">Man perceives it not,</hi> that is, he does not heed it or regard it, does not discern or understand it, is not aware that it is the voice of God, nor does he receive the things revealed, for they are foolishness to him; he stops his ear, stands in his own light, rejects the counsel of God against himself, and so is never the wiser, no not for the dictates of wisdom itself. God speaks to us by conscience, by providences, and by ministers, of all which Elihu here discourses at large, to show Job that God was both telling him his mind and doing him a kindness, even now that he seemed to keep him in the dark and so treat him as a stranger, and to keep him in distress and so treat him as an enemy. There was not then, that we know of, any divine revelation in writing, and therefore that is not here mentioned among the ways by which God speaks to men, though now it is the principal way. <div eID="gen10071" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10072" type="x-p"/> In <reference osisRef="Job.33.14-Job.33.18">these verses</reference> he shows how God teaches and admonishes the children of men by their own consciences. Observe, <div eID="gen10072" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10073" type="x-p"/> I. The proper season and opportunity for these admonitions (<reference osisRef="Job.33.15">v. 15</reference>): <hi type="italic">In a dream, in slumberings upon the bed,</hi> when men are retired from the world and the business and conversation of it. It is a good time for them to retire into their own hearts, and commune with them, when they are upon their beds, solitary and still, <reference osisRef="Ps.4.4">Ps. iv. 4</reference>. It is the time God takes for dealing personally with men. 1. When he sent angels, extraordinary messengers, on his errands, he commonly chose that time for the delivery of their messages, when by deep sleep falling on men the bodily senses were all locked up and the mind more free to receive the immediate communications of divine light. Thus he made his mind known to the prophets by visions and dreams (<reference osisRef="Num.12.6">Num. xii. 6</reference>); thus he warned Abimelech (<reference osisRef="Gen.20.3">Gen. xx. 3</reference>), Laban (<reference osisRef="Gen.31.24">Gen. xxxi. 24</reference>), Joseph (<reference osisRef="Matt.1.20">Matt. i. 20</reference>); thus he made known to Pharaoh and Nebuchadnezzar things that should come to pass hereafter. 2. When he stirred up conscience, that ordinary deputy of his, in the soul, to do its office, he took that opportunity, either when deep sleep fell on men (for, though dreams mostly come from fancy, some may come from conscience) or in slumberings, when men are between sleeping and waking, reflecting at night upon the business of the foregoing day or projecting in the morning the business of the ensuing day; then is a proper time for their hearts to reproach them for what they have done ill and to admonish them what they should do. See <reference osisRef="Isa.30.21">Isa. xxx. 21</reference>. <div eID="gen10073" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10074" type="x-p"/> II. The power and force with which those admonitions come, <reference osisRef="Job.33.16">v. 16</reference>. When God designs men's good by the convictions and dictates of their own consciences, 1. He gives them admission, and makes them to be heeded: <hi type="italic">Then he opens the ears of men,</hi> which were before shut against the voice of this charmer, <reference osisRef="Ps.58.5">Ps. lviii. 5</reference>. He opens the heart, as he opened Lydia's, and so opens the ears. He takes away that which stopped the ear, so that the conviction finds or forces its way; nay, he works in the soul a submission to the regimen of conscience and a compliance with its rules, for that follows upon God's opening the ear, <reference osisRef="Isa.50.5">Isa. l. 5</reference>. <hi type="italic">God has opened my ear, and I was not rebellious.</hi> 2. He gives them a lodgment in the heart and makes them to abide: <hi type="italic">He sealeth their instruction,</hi> that is, the instruction that is designed for them and is suited to them; this he makes their souls to receive the deep and lasting impression of, as the wax of the seal. When the heart is delivered into divine instructions, as into a mould, then the work is done. <div eID="gen10074" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10075" type="x-p"/> III. The end and design of these admonitions that are sent. 1. To keep men from sin, and particularly the sin of pride (<reference osisRef="Job.33.17">v. 17</reference>). <hi type="italic">That he may withdraw man from his purpose,</hi> that is, from his evil purposes, may change the temper of his mind and the course of his life, his disposition and inclination, or prevent some particular sin he is in danger of falling into, that he may withdraw man from his work, may make him leave off man's work, which is working for the world and the flesh, and may set him to work the work of God. Many a man has been stopped in the full career of a sinful pursuit by the seasonable checks of his own conscience, saying, <hi type="italic">Do not this abominable thing which the Lord hates.</hi> Particularly, God does, by this means, <hi type="italic">hide pride from man,</hi> that is, hide those things from him which are the matter of his pride, and take his mind off from dwelling upon them, by setting before him what reason he has to be humble. That he may <hi type="italic">take away pride from man</hi> (so some read it), that he may pluck up that root of bitterness which is the cause of so much sin. All those whom God has mercy in store for he will humble and hide pride from. Pride makes people eager and resolute in the prosecution of their purposes; they will have their way, therefore God withdraws them from their purposes, by mortifying their pride. 2. To keep men from ruin, <reference osisRef="Job.33.18">v. 18</reference>. While sinners are pursuing their evil purposes, and indulging their pride, their souls are hastening apace to the pit, to the sword, to destruction, both in this world and that to come; but when God, by the admonitions of conscience, withdraws them from sin, he thereby <hi type="italic">keeps back</hi> their souls <hi type="italic">from the pit,</hi> from the bottomless pit, and saves them from perishing by <hi type="italic">the sword</hi> of divine vengeance, so iniquity shall not be their ruin. That which turns men from sin saves them from hell, <hi type="italic">saves a soul from death,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jas.5.20">James v. 20</reference>. See what a mercy it is to be under the restraints of an awakened conscience. Faithful are the wounds, and kind are the bonds, of that friend, for by them the soul is kept from perishing eternally.
entries.ab516946d6c801a143811376bcb84a2e9bc1d04b: <div eID="gen10075" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10076" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">19</hi> He is chastened also with pain upon his bed, and the multitude of his bones with strong <hi type="italic">pain:</hi> <hi type="super">20</hi> So that his life abhorreth bread, and his soul dainty meat. <hi type="super">21</hi> His flesh is consumed away, that it cannot be seen; and his bones <hi type="italic">that</hi> were not seen stick out. <hi type="super">22</hi> Yea, his soul draweth near unto the grave, and his life to the destroyers. <hi type="super">23</hi> If there be a messenger with him, an interpreter, one among a thousand, to show unto man his uprightness: <hi type="super">24</hi> Then he is gracious unto him, and saith, Deliver him from going down to the pit: I have found a ransom. <hi type="super">25</hi> His flesh shall be fresher than a child's: he shall return to the days of his youth: <hi type="super">26</hi> He shall pray unto God, and he will be favourable unto him: and he shall see his face with joy: for he will render unto man his righteousness. <hi type="super">27</hi> He looketh upon men, and <hi type="italic">if any</hi> say, I have sinned, and perverted <hi type="italic">that which was</hi> right, and it profited me not; <hi type="super">28</hi> He will deliver his soul from going into the pit, and his life shall see the light. <div eID="gen10076" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10077" type="x-p"/> God has spoken once to sinners by their own consciences, to keep them from the paths of the destroyer, but they perceive it not; they are not aware that the checks their own hearts give them in a sinful way are from God, but they are imputed to melancholy or the preciseness of their education; and therefore God speaks twice; he speaks a second time, and tries another way to convince and reclaim sinners, and that is by providences, afflictive and merciful (in which he speaks twice), and by the seasonable instructions of good ministers setting in with them. Job complained much of his diseases and judged by them that God was angry with him; his friends did so too: but Elihu shows that they were all mistaken, for God often afflicts the body in love, and with gracious designs of good to the soul, as appears in the issue. This part of Elihu's discourse will be of great use to us for the due improvement of sickness, in and by which God speaks to men. Here is, <div eID="gen10077" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10078" type="x-p"/> I. The patient described in his extremity. See what work sickness makes (<reference osisRef="Job.33.19-Job.33.21">v. 19</reference>, &c.) when God sends it with commission. <hi type="italic">Do this, and doeth it.</hi> 1. The sick man is full of pain all over him (<reference osisRef="Job.33.19">v. 19</reference>): <hi type="italic">He is chastened with pain upon his bed,</hi> such pain as confines him to his bed, or so extreme the pain is that he can get no ease, no, not on his bed, where he would repose himself. Pain and sickness will turn a bed of down into a bed of thorns, on which he that used to sleep now tosses to and fro till the dawning of the day. The case, as here put, is very bad. Pain is borne with more difficulty than sickness, and with that the patient here is chastened, not a dull heavy pain, but strong and acute; and frequently the stronger the patient the stronger the pain, for the more sanguine the complexion is the more violent, commonly, the disease is. It is not the smarting of the flesh that is complained of, but the aching of the bones. It is an inward rooted pain; and not only the bones of one limb, but <hi type="italic">the multitude of the bones,</hi> are thus chastened. See what frail, what vile bodies we have, which, though receiving no external hurt, may be thus pained from causes within themselves. See what work sin makes, what mischief it does. Pain is the fruit of sin; yet, by the grace of God, the pain of the body is often made a means of good to the soul. 2. He has quite lost his appetite, the common effect of sickness (<reference osisRef="Job.33.20">v. 20</reference>): <hi type="italic">His life abhorreth bread,</hi> the most necessary food, <hi type="italic">and dainty meat,</hi> which he most delighted in, and formerly relished with a great deal of pleasure. This is a good reason why we should <hi type="italic">not</hi> be <hi type="italic">desirous of dainties, because they are deceitful meat,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.23.3">Prov. xxiii. 3</reference>. We may be soon made as sick of them as we are now fond of them; and those who live in luxury when they are well, if ever they come, by reason of sickness, to loathe dainty meat, may, with grief and shame, read their sin in their punishment. Let us not inordinately love the taste of meat, for the time may come when we may even loathe the sight of meat, <reference osisRef="Ps.107.18">Ps. cvii. 18</reference>. 3. He has become a perfect skeleton, nothing but skin and bones, <reference osisRef="Job.33.21">v. 21</reference>. By sickness, perhaps a few days' sickness, <hi type="italic">his flesh,</hi> which was fat, and fair, <hi type="italic">is consumed away,</hi> that it cannot be seen; it is strangely wasted and gone: <hi type="italic">and his bones,</hi> which were buried in flesh, now <hi type="italic">stick out;</hi> you may count his ribs, may tell all his bones. The soul that is well nourished with the bread of life sickness will not make lean, but it soon makes a change in the body. <div eID="gen10078" type="x-p"/> <lg sID="gen10079"/> <l level="1" sID="gen10080"/>"He who, before, had such a beauteous air,<l eID="gen10080" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen10081"/>And, pampered with the ease, seemed plump and fair<l eID="gen10081" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen10082"/>Doth all his friends (amazing change!) surprise<l eID="gen10082" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen10083"/>With pale lean cheeks and ghastly hollow eyes;<l eID="gen10083" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen10084"/>His bones (a horrid sight) start through his skin,<l eID="gen10084" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen10085"/>Which lay before, in flesh and fat, unseen." Sir <hi type="small-caps">R. Blackmore</hi> .<l eID="gen10085" level="1"/> <lg eID="gen10079"/> <div sID="gen10086" type="x-p"/> 4. He is given up for gone, and his life despaired of (<reference osisRef="Job.33.22">v. 22</reference>): <hi type="italic">His soul draws near to the grave,</hi> that is, he has all the symptoms of death upon him, and in the apprehension of all about him, as well as in his own, he is a dying man. The pangs of death, here called <hi type="italic">the destroyers,</hi> are just ready to seize him; they compass him about, <reference osisRef="Ps.116.3">Ps. cxvi. 3</reference>. Perhaps it intimates the very dreadful apprehensions which those have of death as a destroying thing, when it stares them in the face, who, when it was at a distance, made light of it. All agree when it comes to the point, whatever they thought of it before, that it is a serious thing to die. <div eID="gen10086" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10087" type="x-p"/> II. The provision made for his instruction, in order to a sanctified use of his affliction, that, when God in that way speaks to man, he may be heard and understood, and not speak in vain, <reference osisRef="Job.33.23">v. 23</reference>. He is happy <hi type="italic">if there be a messenger with him</hi> to attend him in his sickness, to convince, counsel, and comfort him, <hi type="italic">an interpreter</hi> to expound the providence and give him to understand the meaning of it, <hi type="italic">a man of wisdom</hi> that knows the voice of the rod and its interpretation; for, when God speaks by afflictions, we are frequently so unversed in the language, that we have need of an interpreter, and it is well if we have such a one. The advice and help of a good minister are as needful and seasonable, and should be as acceptable, in sickness, as of a good physician, especially if he be well skilled in the art of explaining and improving providences; he is then <hi type="italic">one of a thousand,</hi> and to be valued accordingly. His business at such a time is <hi type="italic">to show unto man his uprightness,</hi> that is, God's uprightness, that in faithfulness he afflicts him and does him no wrong, which it is necessary to be convinced of in order to our making a due improvement of the affliction: or, rather, it may mean man's uprightness, or rectitude. 1. The uprightness that <hi type="italic">is.</hi> If it appear that the sick person is truly pious, the interpreter will not do as Job's friends had done, make it his business to prove him a hypocrite because he is afflicted, but on the contrary will show him his uprightness, notwithstanding his afflictions, that he may take the comfort of it, and be easy, whatever the event is. 2. The uprightness, the reformation, that <hi type="italic">should be,</hi> in order to life and peace. When men are made to see the way of uprightness to be the only way, and a sure way to salvation, and to choose it, and walk in it accordingly, the work is done. <div eID="gen10087" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10088" type="x-p"/> III. God's gracious acceptance of him, upon his repentance, <reference osisRef="Job.33.24">v. 24</reference>. When he sees that the sick person is indeed convinced that sincere repentance, and that uprightness which is gospel perfection, are his interest as well as his duty, then he that waits to be gracious, and shows mercy upon the first indication of true repentance, <hi type="italic">is gracious unto him,</hi> and takes him into his favour and thoughts for good. Wherever God finds a gracious heart he will be found a gracious God; and, 1. He will give a gracious order for his discharge. He says, <hi type="italic">Deliver him</hi> (that is, let him be delivered) <hi type="italic">from going down to the pit,</hi> from that death which is the wages of sin. When afflictions have done their work they shall be removed. When we return to God in a way of duty he will return to us in a way of mercy. Those shall be delivered from going down to the pit who receive God's messengers, and rightly understand his interpreters, so as to subscribe to his uprightness. 2. He will give a gracious reason for this order: <hi type="italic">I have found a ransom,</hi> or propitiation; Jesus Christ is that ransom, so Elihu calls him, as Job had called him his Redeemer, for he is both the purchaser and the price, the priest and the sacrifice; so high was the value put upon souls that nothing less would redeem them, and so great the injury done by sin that nothing less would atone for it than the blood of the Son of God, who <hi type="italic">gave his life a ransom for many.</hi> This is a ransom of God's finding, a contrivance of Infinite Wisdom; we could never have found it ourselves, and the angels themselves could never have found it. It is <hi type="italic">the wisdom of God in a mystery, the hidden wisdom,</hi> and such an invention as is and will be the everlasting wonder of those principalities and powers that desire to look into it. Observe how God glories in the invention here, <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">heureka, heureka</hi></hi>—"<hi type="italic">I have found, I have found, the ransom;</hi> I, even I, am he that has done it." <div eID="gen10088" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10089" type="x-p"/> IV. The recovery of the sick man hereupon. Take away the cause and the effect will cease. When the patient becomes a penitent see what a blessed change follows. 1. His body recovers its health, <reference osisRef="Job.33.25">v. 25</reference>. This is not always the consequence of a sick man's repentance and return to God, but sometimes it is; and recovery from sickness is a mercy indeed when it arises from the remission of sin; then it is in love to the soul that the body is <hi type="italic">delivered from the pit of corruption</hi> when God <hi type="italic">casts our sins behind his back,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.38.17">Isa. xxxviii. 17</reference>. That is the method of a blessed recovery. <hi type="italic">Son, be of good cheer, thy sins be forgiven thee;</hi> and then, <hi type="italic">Rise, take up thy bed, and walk,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.9.2">Matt. ix. 2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.9.6">6</reference>. So here, interest him in the ransom, and then <hi type="italic">his flesh shall be fresher than a child's</hi> and there shall be no remains of his distemper, but <hi type="italic">he shall return to the days of his youth,</hi> to the beauty and strength which he had then. When the distemper that oppressed nature is removed how strangely does nature help itself, in which the power and goodness of the God of nature must be thankfully acknowledged! By such merciful providences as these, which afflictions give occasion for, God speaketh once, yea, twice, to the children of men, letting them know (if they would but perceive it) their dependence upon him and his tender compassion of them. 2. His soul recovers it peace, <reference osisRef="Job.33.26">v. 26</reference>. (1.) The patient, being a penitent, is a supplicant, and has learned to pray. He knows God will be sought unto for his favours, and therefore <hi type="italic">he shall pray unto God,</hi> pray for pardon, pray for health. <hi type="italic">Is any afflicted, and sick? Let him pray.</hi> When he finds himself recovering he shall not then think that prayer is no longer necessary, for we need the grace of God as much for the sanctifying of a mercy as for the sanctifying of an affliction. (2.) His prayers are accepted. God <hi type="italic">will be favourable to him,</hi> and be well pleased with him; his anger shall be turned away from him, and the light of God's countenance shall shine upon his soul; and then it follows, (3.) That he has the comfort of communion with God. He shall now see the face of God, which before was hid from him, and he shall see it with joy, for what sight can be more reviving? See <reference osisRef="Gen.33.10">Gen. xxxiii. 10</reference>, <hi type="italic">As though I had seen the face of God.</hi> All true penitents rejoice more in the returns of God's favour than in any instance whatsoever of prosperity or pleasure, <reference osisRef="Ps.4.6-Ps.4.7">Ps. iv. 6, 7</reference>. (4.) He has a blessed tranquility of mind, arising from the sense of his justification before God, who <hi type="italic">will render unto this man his righteousness.</hi> He shall receive the atonement, that is, the comfort of it, <reference osisRef="Rom.5.11">Rom. v. 11</reference>. Righteousness shall be imputed to him, and peace thereupon spoken, the joy and gladness of which he shall then be made to hear though he could not hear them in the day of his affliction. God will now deal with him as a righteous man, with whom it shall be well. He shall <hi type="italic">receive the blessing from the Lord, even righteousness,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.24.5">Ps. xxiv. 5</reference>. God shall give him grace to go and sin no more. Perhaps this may denote the reformation of his life after his recovery. As he shall pray unto God, whom before he had slighted, so he shall render to man his righteousness, whom before he had wronged, shall make restitution, and for the future do justly. <div eID="gen10089" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10090" type="x-p"/> V. The general rule which God will go by in dealing with the children of men inferred from this instance, <reference osisRef="Job.33.27-Job.33.28">v. 27, 28</reference>. As sick people, upon their submission, are restored, so all others that truly repent of their sins shall find mercy with God. See here, 1. What sin is, and what reason we have not to sin. Would we know the nature of sin and the malignity of it? It is the perverting of that which is right; it is a most unjust unreasonable thing; it is the rebellion of the creature against the Creator, the usurped dominion of the flesh over the spirit, and a contradiction to the eternal rules and reasons of good and evil. It is <hi type="italic">perverting the right ways of the Lord</hi> (<reference osisRef="Acts.13.10">Acts xiii. 10</reference>), and therefore the ways of sin are called <hi type="italic">crooked ways,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.125.5">Ps. cxxv. 5</reference>. Would we know what is to be got by sin? <hi type="italic">It profiteth us not.</hi> The works of darkness are unfruitful works. When profit and loss come to be balanced all the gains of sin, put them all together, will come far short of countervailing the damage. All true penitents are ready to own this, and it is a mortifying consideration. <reference osisRef="Rom.6.21">Rom. vi. 21</reference>, <hi type="italic">What fruit had you then in those things whereof you are now ashamed?</hi> 2. See what repentance is, and what reason we have to repent. Would we approve ourselves true penitents? We must then, with a broken and contrite heart, confess our sins to God, <reference osisRef="1John.1.9">1 John i. 9</reference>. We must confess the fact of sin (<hi type="italic">I have sinned</hi>) and not deny the charge, or stand upon our own justification; we must confess the fault of sin, the iniquity, the dishonesty of it ( <hi type="italic">have perverted that which was right</hi>); we must confess the folly of sin—"so foolish have I been and ignorant, for <hi type="italic">it profited me not;</hi> and therefore what have I to do any more with it?" Is there not good reason why we should make such a penitent confession as this? For, (1.) God expect it. <hi type="italic">He looks upon men,</hi> when they have sinned, to see what they will do next, whether they will go on in it or whether they will bethink themselves and return. He hearkens and hears whether any say, <hi type="italic">What have I done?</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.8.6">Jer. viii. 6</reference>. He looks upon sinners with an eye of compassion, desiring to hear this from them; for he has no pleasure in their ruin. He looks upon them, and, as soon as he perceives these workings of repentance in them, he encourages them and is ready to accept them (<reference osisRef="Ps.32.5-Ps.32.6">Ps. xxxii. 5, 6</reference>), as the father went forth to meet the returning prodigal. (2.) It will turn to our unspeakable advantage. The promise is general. If any humble himself thus, whoever he be, [1.] He shall not come into condemnation, but be saved from the wrath to come: <hi type="italic">He shall deliver his soul from going into the pit,</hi> the pit of hell; iniquity shall not be his ruin. [2.] He shall be happy in everlasting life and joy: <hi type="italic">His life shall see the light,</hi> that is, all good, in the vision and fruition of God. To obtain this bliss, if the prophet had bidden us do some great thing, would we not have done it? How much more when he only says unto us, <hi type="italic">Wash and be clean,</hi> confess and be pardoned, repent and be saved?
entries.2607fa4d606ffd35b40d94db7c3c13ae684c54a2: <div eID="gen10090" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10091" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">29</hi> Lo, all these <hi type="italic">things</hi> worketh God oftentimes with man, <hi type="super">30</hi> To bring back his soul from the pit, to be enlightened with the light of the living. <hi type="super">31</hi> Mark well, O Job, hearken unto me: hold thy peace, and I will speak. 32 If thou hast any thing to say, answer me: speak, for I desire to justify thee. <hi type="super">33</hi> If not, hearken unto me: hold thy peace, and I shall teach thee wisdom. <div eID="gen10091" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10092" type="x-p"/> We have here the conclusion of this first part of Elihu's discourse, in which, 1. He briefly sums up what he had said, showing that God's great and gracious design, in all the dispensations of his providence towards the children of men, is to save them from being for ever miserable and bring them to be for ever happy, <reference osisRef="Job.33.29-Job.33.30">v. 29, 30</reference>. <hi type="italic">All these things God is working with the children of men.</hi> He deals with them by conscience, by providences, by ministers, by mercies, by afflictions. He makes them sick, and makes them well again. All these are his operations; he has <hi type="italic">set the one over the other</hi> (<reference osisRef="Eccl.7.14">Eccl. vii. 14</reference>), but his hand is in all; it is he that performs all the things for us. All providences are to be looked upon as God's workings with man, his strivings with him. He uses a variety of methods to do men good; if one affliction do not do the work, he will try another; if neither do, he will try a mercy; and he will send a messenger to interpret both. He often works such things as these twice, thrice; so it is in the original, referring to <reference osisRef="Job.33.14">v. 14</reference>. He <hi type="italic">speaks once, yea, twice;</hi> if that prevail not, he works twice, yea, thrice; he changes his method (<hi type="italic">we have piped, we have mourned</hi>) returns again to the same method, repeats the same applications. Why does he take all this pains with man? It is <hi type="italic">to bring back his soul from the pit,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.33.30">v. 30</reference>. If God did not take more care of us than we do of ourselves, we should be miserable; we would destroy ourselves, but he would have us saved, and devises means, by his grace, to undo that by which we were undoing ourselves. The former method, by dream and vision, was to <hi type="italic">keep back the soul from the pit</hi> (<reference osisRef="Job.33.18">v. 18</reference>), that is, to prevent sin, that we might not fall into it. This, by sickness and the word, is to bring back the soul, to recover those that have fallen into sin, that they may not lie still and perish in it. With respect to all that by repentance are brought back from the pit, it is that they may be <hi type="italic">enlightened with the light of the living,</hi> that they may have present comfort and everlasting happiness. Whom God saves from sin and hell, which are darkness, he will bring to heaven, the inheritance of the saints in light; and this he aims at in all his institutions and all his dispensations. <hi type="italic">Lord, what is man, that thou shouldst thus visit him!</hi> This should engage us to comply with God's designs, to work with him for our own good, and not to counter-work him. This will render those that perish for ever inexcusable, that so much was done to save them and they would not be healed. 2. He bespeaks Job's acceptance of what he had offered and begs of him to <hi type="italic">mark it well,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.33.31">v. 31</reference>. What is intended for our good challenges our regard. If Job will observe what is said, (1.) He is welcome to make what objections he can against it (<reference osisRef="Job.33.32">v. 32</reference>): "<hi type="italic">If thou hast any thing to say</hi> for thyself, in thy own vindication, <hi type="italic">answer me;</hi> though I am fresh, and thou art spent, I will not run thee down with words: <hi type="italic">Speak, for I, desire to justify thee,</hi> and am not as thy other friends that desired to condemn thee." Elihu contends for truth, not, as they did, for victory. Note, Those we reprove we should desire to justify, and be glad to see them clear themselves from the imputations they lie under, and therefore give them all possible advantage and encouragement to do so. (2.) If he has nothing to say against what is said, Elihu lets him know that he has something more to say, which he desires him patiently to attend to (<reference osisRef="Job.33.33">v. 33</reference>): <hi type="italic">Hold thy peace, and I will teach thee wisdom.</hi> Those that would both show wisdom and learn wisdom must hearken and keep silence, be swift to hear and slow to speak. Job was wise and good; but those that are so may yet be wiser and better, and must therefore set themselves to improve by the means of wisdom and grace.  <chapter eID="Job.33"/> <div eID="gen10092" type="x-p"/>

entries.fa66e3caab163c2d97244b75dd2b9876204b4d3d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5183"/><div sID="gen7718" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5183"/><hi type="bold">4. The Spirit of God hath made me--</hi>as He did thee: latter clause of <reference osisRef="Job.33.6">Job 33:6</reference> (<reference osisRef="Gen.2.7">Ge 2:7</reference>). Therefore thou needest not fear me, as thou wouldest God (<reference osisRef="Job.33.7">Job 33:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.9.34">Job 9:34</reference>). On the other hand, "the breath of the Almighty hath inspired me" (as <reference osisRef="Job.32.8">Job 32:8</reference>); not as English Version, "given me life"; therefore "I am according to thy wish (<reference osisRef="Job.9.32">Job 9:32</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.9.33">33</reference>) in God's stead" to thee; a "daysman," umpire, or mediator, between God and thee. So Elihu was designed by the Holy Ghost to be a type of Jesus Christ (<reference osisRef="Job.33.23-Job.33.26">Job 33:23-26</reference>). <div eID="gen7718" type="x-p"/>

entries.f38a9ce4291af0d19cdd3c5dc586443f207fe556: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5185"/><div sID="gen7721" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5185"/>6. (See on <reference osisRef="Job.33.4">Job 33:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.31.35">Job 31:35</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.13.3">13:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.20.21">20, 21</reference>).<div eID="gen7721" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7722" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">formed--</hi>Though acting as God's representative, I am but a creature, like thyself. Arabic, "pressed together," as a mass of clay by the potter, in forming a vessel [Umbreit]. Hebrew, "cut off," as the portion taken from the clay to form it [Maurer]. <div eID="gen7722" type="x-p"/>
entries.48e731b986d245d86aab4b793ee20af29a46b2e1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5186"/><div sID="gen7723" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5186"/><hi type="bold">7. hand--</hi>alluding to Job's words (<reference osisRef="Job.13.21">Job 13:21</reference>). <div eID="gen7723" type="x-p"/>
entries.9d3446880ea490f8aee6c76c0b1c1f49afa2707a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5187"/><div sID="gen7724" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5187"/><hi type="bold">8. thy words--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Job.10.7">Job 10:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.16.17">16:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.23.11">23:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.23.12">12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.27.5">27:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.27.6">6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.29.14">29:14</reference>). In <reference osisRef="Job.9.30">Job 9:30</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.13.23">13:23</reference>, Job had acknowledged sin; but the general spirit of his words was to maintain himself to be "clean," and to charge God with injustice. He went too far on the opposite side in opposing the friends' false charge of hypocrisy. Even the godly, though willing to confess themselves sinners in general, often dislike sin in particular to be brought as a charge against them. Affliction is therefore needed to bring them to feel that sin in them deserves even worse than they suffer and that God does them no injustice. Then at last humbled under God they find, affliction is for their real good, and so at last it is taken away either here, or at least at death. To teach this is Elihu's mission. <div eID="gen7724" type="x-p"/>
entries.02bfd5aaf11468ad114e35b8abbd6d1ee705fdd3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5188"/><div sID="gen7725" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5188"/><hi type="bold">9. clean--</hi>spotless. <div eID="gen7725" type="x-p"/>
entries.86f17361f736a51c96d3babcdba2ee1acb341f0a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5189"/><div sID="gen7726" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5189"/><hi type="bold">10. occasions--</hi>for hostility; literally, "enmities" (<reference osisRef="Job.13.24">Job 13:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.16.9">16:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.19.11">19:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.30.21">30:21</reference>). <div eID="gen7726" type="x-p"/>
entries.62dbd76a66366d133e5729ba9f93518e53372e9d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5190"/><div sID="gen7727" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5190"/>11. (<reference osisRef="Job.13.27">Job 13:27</reference>).<div eID="gen7727" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7728" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">marketh--</hi>narrowly watches (<reference osisRef="Job.14.16">Job 14:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.7.12">7:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.31.4">31:4</reference>). <div eID="gen7728" type="x-p"/>
entries.dea9990f3cc0024379492f020228d29e6c582ba3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5191"/><div sID="gen7729" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5191"/><hi type="bold">12. in this--</hi>view of God and His government. It cannot be that God should jealously "watch" man, though "spotless," as an "enemy," or as one afraid of him as an equal. For "God is greater than man!" There must be sin in man, even though he be no hypocrite, which needs correction by suffering for the sufferer's good. <div eID="gen7729" type="x-p"/>
entries.56e4e55a15973fa42bcf2b7d4ecf6cb313ff140a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5192"/><div sID="gen7730" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5192"/>13. (<reference osisRef="Isa.45.9">Is 45:9</reference>).<div eID="gen7730" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7731" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">his matters--</hi>ways. Our part is, not to "strive" with God, but to submit. To believe it is right because He does it, not because we see all the reasons for His doing it. <div eID="gen7731" type="x-p"/>
entries.9854ccea1340f833ec065faa1515183d0c7867aa: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5193"/><div sID="gen7732" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5193"/><hi type="bold">14. Translate, "Yet, man regardeth it not"; or rather, as Umbreit, "Yea, twice (He repeats the warning)--</hi>if man gives no heed" to the first warning. Elihu implies that God's reason for sending affliction is because, when God has communicated His will in various ways, man in prosperity has not heeded it; God therefore must try what affliction will effect (<reference osisRef="John.15.2">Joh 15:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.62.11">Psa 62:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.28.10">Is 28:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.28.13">13</reference>). <div eID="gen7732" type="x-p"/>
entries.c1697de4fb0512bb040ef716d3b3915c1d74d17f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5194"/><div sID="gen7733" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5194"/><hi type="bold">15. slumberings--</hi>light is opposed to "deep sleep." Elihu has in view Eliphaz (<reference osisRef="Job.4.13">Job 4:13</reference>), and also Job himself (<reference osisRef="Job.7.14">Job 7:14</reference>). "Dreams" in sleep, and "visions" of actual apparitions, were among the ways whereby God then spake to man (<reference osisRef="Gen.20.3">Ge 20:3</reference>). <div eID="gen7733" type="x-p"/>
entries.b86095561c6d28de652e1a5c7e4bc955f7b3b49d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5195"/><div sID="gen7734" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5195"/>16. Literally, "sealeth (their ears) to Himself by warnings," that is, with the sureness and secrecy of a seal He reveals His warnings [Umbreit]. To seal up securely (<reference osisRef="Job.37.7">Job 37:7</reference>). <div eID="gen7734" type="x-p"/>
entries.ca2cb5efd4ecb0eb3471497214f4e0b23ae8a28e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5196"/><div sID="gen7735" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5196"/><hi type="bold">17. purpose--</hi>Margin, "work." So <reference osisRef="Job.36.9">Job 36:9</reference>. So "business" in a bad sense (<reference osisRef="1Sam.20.19">1Sa 20:19</reference>). Elihu alludes to Job's words (<reference osisRef="Job.17.11">Job 17:11</reference>). "Pride," an open "pit" (<reference osisRef="Job.33.18">Job 33:18</reference>) which God hides or covers up, lest man should fall into it. Even the godly need to learn the lesson which trials teach, to "humble themselves under the mighty hand of God." <div eID="gen7735" type="x-p"/>
entries.8cb2084efd2b92aff26266a4a26ae35b053bf15d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5197"/><div sID="gen7736" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5197"/><hi type="bold">18. his soul--</hi>his life.<div eID="gen7736" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7737" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the pit--</hi>the grave; a symbol of hell.<div eID="gen7737" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7738" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">perishing by the sword--</hi>that is, a violent death; in the Old Testament a symbol of the future punishment of the ungodly. <div eID="gen7738" type="x-p"/>
entries.b6b61a1fc1174410a95ab8117177db3744aef0b1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5198"/><div sID="gen7739" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5198"/>19. When man does not heed warnings of the night, he is chastened, &c. The new thought suggested by Elihu is that affliction is disciplinary (<reference osisRef="Job.36.10">Job 36:10</reference>); for the good of the godly.<div eID="gen7739" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7740" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">multitude--</hi>so the Margin, Hebrew (Keri). Better with the text (Chetib), "And with the perpetual (strong) contest of his bones"; the never-resting fever in his bones (<reference osisRef="Ps.38.3">Psa 38:3</reference>) [Umbreit]. <div eID="gen7740" type="x-p"/>
entries.8cd829024ba2d42b872ff25e08af58b21c4774b0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5199"/><div sID="gen7741" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5199"/><hi type="bold">20. life--</hi>that is, the appetite, which ordinarily sustains "life" (<reference osisRef="Job.38.39">Job 38:39</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.107.18">Psa 107:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eccl.12.5">Ec 12:5</reference>). The taking away of desire for food by sickness symbolizes the removal by affliction of lust, for things which foster the spiritual fever of pride.<div eID="gen7741" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7742" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">soul--</hi>desire. <div eID="gen7742" type="x-p"/>
entries.8ea1f928844af1366905849898fd8d79232d0473: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5200"/><div sID="gen7743" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5200"/>21. His flesh once prominent "can no more be seen." His bones once not seen now appear prominent.<div eID="gen7743" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7744" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">stick out--</hi>literally, "are bare." The Margin, Hebrew (Keri) reading. The text (Chetib) reads it a noun "(are become) bareness." The Keri was no doubt an explanatory reading of transcribers. <div eID="gen7744" type="x-p"/>
entries.602fa31eaeeb92df337fe53598772529cd093a77: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5201"/><div sID="gen7745" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5201"/><hi type="bold">22. destroyers--</hi>angels of death commissioned by God to end man's life (<reference osisRef="2Sam.24.16">2Sa 24:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.78.49">Psa 78:49</reference>). The death pains personified may, however, be meant; so "gnawers" (see on <reference osisRef="Job.30.17">Job 30:17</reference>). <div eID="gen7745" type="x-p"/>
entries.448c4cf951dbed0d4d1e9d578280e5c61002813b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5202"/><div sID="gen7746" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5202"/>23. Elihu refers to himself as the divinely-sent (<reference osisRef="Job.32.8">Job 32:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.33.6">33:6</reference>) "messenger," the "interpreter" to explain to Job and vindicate God's righteousness; such a one Eliphaz had denied that Job could look for (<reference osisRef="Job.5.1">Job 5:1</reference>), and Job (<reference osisRef="Job.9.33">Job 9:33</reference>) had wished for such a "daysman" or umpire between him and God. The "messenger" of good is antithetical to the "destroyers" (<reference osisRef="Job.33.23">Job 33:23</reference>).<div eID="gen7746" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7747" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">with him--</hi>if there be vouchsafed to the sufferer. The office of the interpreter is stated "to show unto man God's uprightness" in His dealings; or, as Umbreit, "man's upright course towards God" (<reference osisRef="Prov.14.2">Pr 14:2</reference>). The former is better; Job maintained his own "uprightness" (<reference osisRef="Job.16.17">Job 16:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.27.5">27:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.27.6">6</reference>); Elihu on the contrary maintains God's, and that man's true uprightness lies in submission to God. "One among a thousand" is a man rarely to be found. So Jesus Christ (<reference osisRef="Song.5.10">So 5:10</reference>). Elihu, the God-sent mediator of a temporal deliverance, is a type of the God-man Jesus Christ the Mediator of eternal deliverance: "the messenger of the covenant" (Mal 3:1). This is the wonderful work of the Holy Ghost, that persons and events move in their own sphere in such a way as unconsciously to shadow forth Him, whose "testimony is the Spirit of prophecy"; as the same point may be center of a small and of a vastly larger concentric circle. <div eID="gen7747" type="x-p"/>
entries.1e80631eaab7ce4112917e9f6eb6c26eb6f10b72: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5203"/><div sID="gen7748" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5203"/>24. Apodosis to <reference osisRef="Job.33.23">Job 33:23</reference>.<div eID="gen7748" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7749" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">he--</hi>God.<div eID="gen7749" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7750" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Deliver--</hi>literally, "redeem"; in it and "ransom" there is reference to the consideration, on account of which God pardons and relieves the sufferers; here it is primarily the intercession of Elihu. But the language is too strong for its full meaning to be exhausted by this. The Holy Ghost has suggested language which receives its full realization only in the "eternal redemption found" by God in the price paid by Jesus Christ for it; that is, His blood and meritorious intercession (<reference osisRef="Heb.9.12">He 9:12</reference>). "Obtained," literally, "found"; implying the earnest zeal, wisdom, and faithfulness of the finder, and the newness and joyousness of the finding. Jesus Christ could not but have found it, but still His seeking it was needed [Bengel], (<reference osisRef="Luke.15.8">Lu 15:8</reference>). God the Father, is the Finder (<reference osisRef="Ps.89.19">Psa 89:19</reference>). Jesus Christ the Redeemer, to whom He saith, Redeem (so Hebrew) him from going, &c. (<reference osisRef="2Cor.5.19">2Co 5:19</reference>).<div eID="gen7750" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7751" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">ransom--</hi>used in a general sense by Elihu, but meant by the Holy Ghost in its strict sense as applied to Jesus Christ, of a price paid for deliverance (<reference osisRef="Exod.21.30">Ex 21:30</reference>), an atonement (that is, means of selling at once, that is, reconciling "two" who are estranged), a covering, as of the ark with pitch, typical of what covers us sinners from wrath (<reference osisRef="Gen.6.14">Ge 6:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.32.1">Psa 32:1</reference>). The pit is primarily here the grave (<reference osisRef="Isa.38.17">Is 38:17</reference>), but the spiritual pit is mainly shadowed forth (<reference osisRef="Zech.9.11">Zec 9:11</reference>). <div eID="gen7751" type="x-p"/>
entries.3105b0b452e31612db82c4a08c21dc82a370d2c9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5204"/><div sID="gen7752" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5204"/>25-28. Effects of restoration to God's favor; literally, to Job a temporal revival; spiritually, an eternal regeneration. The striking words cannot be restricted to their temporal meaning, as used by Elihu (<reference osisRef="1Pet.1.11">1Pe 1:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.12">12</reference>).<div eID="gen7752" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7753" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">his flesh shall be fresher than a child's--</hi>so Naaman, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.5.14">2Ki 5:14</reference>, spiritually, <reference osisRef="John.3.3-John.3.7">Joh 3:3-7</reference>. <div eID="gen7753" type="x-p"/>
entries.a1973af762cd4a7998129a2b71561c93da7a4a04: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5208"/><div sID="gen7764" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5208"/>29. Margin, "twice and thrice," alluding to <reference osisRef="Job.33.14">Job 33:14</reference>; once, by visions, <reference osisRef="Job.33.15-Job.33.17">Job 33:15-17</reference>; secondly, by afflictions, <reference osisRef="Job.33.19-Job.33.22">Job 33:19-22</reference>; now, by the "messenger," thirdly, <reference osisRef="Job.33.23">Job 33:23</reference>. <div eID="gen7764" type="x-p"/>
entries.c226cb069f7536487adcfcb47138361438e5a7d5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5209"/><div sID="gen7765" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5209"/>30. Referring to <reference osisRef="Job.33.28">Job 33:28</reference> (<reference osisRef="Ps.50.13">Psa 50:13</reference>). <div eID="gen7765" type="x-p"/>
entries.2fd1f60d4c216ee94a6228d2399e67f4a6ea7537: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5210"/><div sID="gen7766" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5210"/><hi type="bold">32. justify--</hi>to do thee justice; and, if I can, consistently with it, to declare thee innocent. At <reference osisRef="Job.33.33">Job 33:33</reference> Elihu pauses for a reply; then proceeds in <reference osisRef="Job.34.1">Job 34:1</reference>. <chapter eID="Job.33"/>

entries.fe0ef63e6ebc4085152bc87382d791adc18a2d0b: <div eID="gen17565" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen17566" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen17567" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen17567" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen17566" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen17568" type="x-p"/> Elihu offers himself in God's stead to reason with Job in meekness and sincerity, <reference osisRef="Job.33.1-Job.33.7">Job 33:1-7</reference>. Charges Job with irreverent expressions, <reference osisRef="Job.33.8-Job.33.12">Job 33:8-12</reference>. Vindicates the providence of God, and shows the various methods which he uses to bring sinners to himself: - By dreams and visions, <reference osisRef="Job.33.13-Job.33.15">Job 33:13-15</reference>; by secret inspirations, <reference osisRef="Job.33.16-Job.33.18">Job 33:16-18</reference>; by afflictions, <reference osisRef="Job.33.19-Job.33.22">Job 33:19-22</reference>; by messengers of righteousness, <reference osisRef="Job.33.23">Job 33:23</reference>; and by the great atonement, <reference osisRef="Job.33.24">Job 33:24</reference>. How and from what God redeems men, and the blessings which he communicates, <reference osisRef="Job.33.25-Job.33.30">Job 33:25-30</reference>. Job is exhorted to listen attentively to Elihu's teaching, <reference osisRef="Job.33.31-Job.33.33">Job 33:31-33</reference>.
entries.e321485fc141741bc281beb675ba3a414ca28f09: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen17568" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17569" type="x-p"/> My words shall be of the uprightness - As God has given me his Spirit, from that Spirit alone will I speak; therefore all my words shall be of uprightness, knowledge, and truth. <div eID="gen17569" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17570" type="x-p"/> Knowledge clearly - דעת ברור daath barur, pure science. I shall lay down no false positions, and I shall have no false consequences.
entries.47928c007329e4a96de4ac32cc8f9c8810974fd7: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen17570" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17571" type="x-p"/> The Spirit of God hath made me - Another plain allusion to the account of the creation of man, <reference osisRef="Gen.2.7">Gen 2:7</reference>, as the words נשמת nishmath, the breath or breathing of God, and תחיני techaiyeni, hath given me life, prove: "He breathed into his nostrils the breath of lives, and he became a living soul."
entries.e4f7829e2c32d07c2a0e739caca7736380d27a7d: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen17571" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17572" type="x-p"/> I am according to thy wish in God's stead: I also am formed out of the clay - Mr. Good, and before him none other that I have seen, has most probably hit the true meaning: - "Behold, I am thy fellow. <div eID="gen17572" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17573" type="x-p"/> I too was formed by God out of the clay." <div eID="gen17573" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17574" type="x-p"/> The word כפיך kephicha, which we translate according to thy wish, and which, if Hebrew, would mean like to thy mouth; he considers as pure Arabic, with a Hebrew postfix, (Arabic) kefoo, signifying fellow, equal, like. Taken in this way, the passage is very plain, only לאל lael, by or through God, must be added to the last clause of the verse instead of the first, as Mr. Good has properly done.
entries.580782e792d3dc00ba6e5671b28616e18c29f415: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen17574" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17575" type="x-p"/> My terror shall not make thee afraid - This is an allusion to what Job had said, <reference osisRef="Job.9.34">Job 9:34</reference> : "Let him take his rod away from me, and let not his fear terrify me." Being thy equal, no fear can impose upon thee so far as to overawe thee; so that thou shouldst not be able to conduct thy own defense. We are on equal terms; now prepare to defend thyself.
entries.78a99ee4e55de2c689e8d61617ae63282f39d4ed: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen17575" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17576" type="x-p"/> Surely thou hast spoken - What Elihu speaks here, and in the three following verses, contains, in general, simple quotations from Job's own words, or the obvious sense of them, as the reader may see by referring to <reference osisRef="Job.13.27">Job 13:27</reference> (note); <reference osisRef="Job.14.16">Job 14:16</reference> (note), and <reference osisRef="Job.31.4">Job 31:4</reference> (note), and also to the notes on those passages.
entries.a197e5f489ac7d64b772cde5573f40167059ce37: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen17576" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17577" type="x-p"/> He putteth my feet in the stocks - See the note on <reference osisRef="Job.13.27">Job 13:27</reference>.
entries.162818c70058f4d7c5aa9b677baef9be1290db74: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen17577" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17578" type="x-p"/> In this thou art not just - Thou hast laid charges against God's dealings, but thou hast not been able to justify those charges; and were there nothing else against thee, these irreverent speeches are so many proofs that thou art not clear in the sight of God.
entries.6b483b598b04460a4e1cd0433c2e29b6ff73d5d0: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen17578" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17579" type="x-p"/> Why dost thou strive against him? - Is it not useless to contend with God? Can he do any thing that is not right? As to his giving thee any account of the reasons why he deals thus and thus with thee, or any one else, thou needest not expect it; he is sovereign, and is not to be called to the bar of his creatures. It is sufficient for thee to know that "he is too wise to err, and too good to be unkind."
entries.2938ee957c6f94adf50adc1cd2f2f9083eaa027b: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen17579" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17580" type="x-p"/> For God speaketh once - Though he will not be summoned to the bar of his creatures, nor condescend to detail the reasons of his conduct, which they could not comprehend, yet he so acts, in the main, that the operation of his hand and the designs of his counsel may sufficiently appear, provided men had their eyes open upon his ways, and their hearts open to receive his influence. Elihu, having made the general statement that God would not come to the bar of his creatures to give account of his conduct, shows the general means which he uses to bring men to an acquaintance with themselves and with him: he states these in the six following particulars, which may be collected from <reference osisRef="Job.33.15-Job.33.24">Job 33:15-24</reference>.
entries.7bb4a362f0962c12b970506542d6e5d8eb28d3b0: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen17580" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17581" type="x-p"/> I. In a Dream <div eID="gen17581" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17582" type="x-p"/> In a Dream - when deep sleep falleth upon men - Many, by such means, have had the most salutary warnings; and to decry all such, because there are many vain dreams, would be nearly as much wisdom as to deny the Bible, because there are many foolish books, the authors of which supposed they were under a Divine influence while composing them. <div eID="gen17582" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17583" type="x-p"/> II. In a Vision <div eID="gen17583" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17584" type="x-p"/> In a Vision of the night - in slumberings upon the bed - Visions or images presented in the imagination during slumber, when men are betwixt sleeping and waking, or when, awake and in bed, they are wrapt up in deep contemplation, the darkness of the night having shut out all objects from their sight, so that the mind is not diverted by images of earthly things impressed on the senses. Many warnings in this way have come from God; and the impression they made, and the good effect they produced, were the proofs of their Divine origin. To deny this would be to call into doubt the testimony of the best, wisest, and holiest men in all ages of the Church. Of one of these visions we have a remarkable account in this book, <reference osisRef="Job.4.12-Job.4.21">Job 4:12-21</reference>. And this vision seems to have taken place in the night season, when Eliphaz awoke from a deep sleep. There is this difference between the accidents of the dream and the vision: the former takes place when deep sleep falleth upon men; the latter, in the night, in or after slumberings upon the bed.
entries.454c130ef47c11c52776f60adc97ad4eaeaa1fdf: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen17584" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17585" type="x-p"/> III. By secret Inspirations <div eID="gen17585" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17586" type="x-p"/> Then he openeth the ears of men, and sealeth, etc. - A dream or a vision simply considered is likely to do no good; it is the opening of the understanding, and the pouring in of the light, that make men wise to salvation.
