One of the old writers<note placement="foot">Jacob Hoffmann (of St. Gallen), <hi type="italic">Gedult Iobs,</hi> Basel, 1663 (a rare little book which I became acquainted with in the town library of St. Gallen).</note> says, “Elihu proves that it can indeed be that a man may fear and honour God from the heart, and consequently be in favour with God, and still be heavily visited by God, either for a trial of faith, hope, and patience, or for the revelation and improvement of the sinful blemishes which now and then are also hidden from the pious.” According to this, both aspects are found united in Elihu’s speeches; but in this first speech, at least, we cannot find it. <div eID="gen8410" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8411" type="x-p"/> There is another poet, whose <hi type="italic">charisma</hi> does not come up to that of the older poet, who in this speech pursues the well-authorized purpose not only of moderating what is extreme in Job’s speeches, but also of bringing out what is true in the speeches of the friends.<note placement="foot">On this subject see my Art. <hi type="italic">Hiob</hi> in Herzog’s <hi type="italic">Real-Encyklopädie</hi>, vi. 116-119, and comp. Kahnis, <hi type="italic">Dogmatik</hi>, i. 306-309, and my <hi type="italic">Für und wider Kahnis</hi> (1863), S. 19-21.</note> <div eID="gen8411" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8412" type="x-p"/> While the book of Job, apart from these speeches, presents in the Old Testament way the great truth which Paul, <reference osisRef="Rom.8.1">Rom 8:1</reference>, expresses in the words, οὐδέν κατάκριμα τοῖς ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ, this other poet has given expression at the same time, in the connection of the drama, to the great truth, <reference osisRef="1Cor.11.32">1Co 11:32</reference>, κρινόμενοι ὑπὸ τοῦ δυρίου παιδευόμεθα, ἵνα μὴ σὺν τῷ κόσμῳ κατακριθῶμεν. That it is another poet, is already manifest from his inferior, or if it is preferred, different, poetic gift. True, A. B. Davidson has again recently asserted, that by supporting it by such observations, the critical question is made “a question of subjective taste.” But if these speeches and the other parts of the book are said to have been written by <hi type="italic">one</hi> poet, there is an end to all critical judgment in such questions generally. One cannot avoid the impression of the distance between them; and if it be suppressed for a time, it will nevertheless make itself constantly felt. But do the prophecies of Malachi stand lower in the scale of the historical development of revelation, because the Salomonic glory of prophetic speech which we admire in Isaiah is wanting in them? Just as little do we depreciate the spiritual glory of these speeches, when we find the outward glory of the rest of the book wanting in them. They occupy a position of the highest worth in the historical development of revelation and redemption. They are a perfecting part of the canonical Scriptures. In their origin, also, they are not much later;<note placement="foot">Seinecke (<hi type="italic">Der Grundgedanke</hi> <hi type="italic">des B. Hiob,</hi> 1863) places it, with Ewald, 100-200 years later; and, moreover, asserts that the book of Job has no foundation whatever in oral tradition - Job is the Israel of the exile, Uz is Judaea, etc.</note> indeed, I venture to assert that they are by a contemporary member even of the Chokma-fellowship from which the book of Job has its rise. For they stand in like intimate relation with the rest of the book to the two Ezrahite Psalms, 88, 89; they have, as to their doctrinal contents, the fundamental features of the Israelitish Chokma in common; they speak another and still similar Aramaizing and Arabizing language (<hi type="italic">hebraicum arabicumque sermonem et interdum syrum,</hi> as Jerome expresses it in his <hi type="italic">Praef. in l. Iobi</hi>); in fact, we shall further on meet with linguistic signs that the poet who wrote this addition has lived together with the poet of the book of Job in one spot beyond the Holy Land, and speaks a Hebrew bearing traces of a like dialectic influence.  <chapter eID="Job.33"/> <div eID="gen8412" type="x-p"/>

And then he shall acknowledge God's great goodness to him, and shall add what follows in the next Verse, <ns0:hi>He hath delivered my Soul,</ns0:hi> &c. <ns0:hi>and my life,</ns0:hi> &c. as they render it. Or rather 2. God diligently observes all Mankind and their several carriages, especially in sickness and distress.</ns0:note>, <ns0:hi>and</ns0:hi> if <ns0:hi>any</ns0:hi> say, I have sinned <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">If there be any Man that sincerely saith thus, God hears it and will pardon, and heal him, as it follows.</ns0:note> and perverted that which was right <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">Either 1. I have judged perversly of the just and right ways of God, cen<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />suring his proceedings against me as too severe and rigorous, whereas in truth I only was to be blamed. Or 2. I have perverted God's righteous Law by bending it, and making it comply with my crooked ways<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> Or, I have swerved from the right and good way of God's commands: or, I have made crooked paths. So he re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />peats in other words what he said in the former branch of the Verse, <ns0:hi>I have sinned.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note>, and it profited me not <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">I got no good by so doing, as I vainly promised my self, but I got much hurt by it, even diseases and griefs and extreme dangers. This was the just fruit of my sins. It is a <ns0:hi>Meiosis</ns0:hi> whereby less is said and more is understood, of which we have seen many examples before.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>

                     </ns0:note> from going into the pit, and his life <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">See on <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 18.</ns0:note> shall see the light <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Shall enjoy either 1. pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sperity, which is oft called <ns0:hi>light,</ns0:hi> as <ns0:hi>darkness</ns0:hi> is put for affliction, or 2. <ns0:hi>the light of the living,</ns0:hi> as it follows <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 30. the light of this World, <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> His life which was endangered, shall be restored and continued.                   <ns0:p n="29">29. Lo, all these things worketh God <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">All these ways and methods doth God use to awaken and con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vince and save sinners.</ns0:note>

                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> That he may enjoy the light of life, and continue in the Land of the Living, out of which he was going.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="31">31. Mark well, O Job, hearken unto me, hold thy peace <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">Attend to what I have further to say to thee with patience and silence.</ns0:note>, and I will speak.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="32">32. If thou hast any thing to say <ns0:hi>i,</ns0:hi> answer me: speak, for I desire to justifie thee <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">For thy own justification, or in answer to the charge that I have already brought against thee.</ns0:note> 
                     <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">To wit, as far as may con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sist with Truth and Justice. I do not speak with evil design, or a bitter mind, or as one resolved to condemn thee whatsoever thou sayest, and I shall be glad to hear any thing from thee, which may make for thy just vindication.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
